items.name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
items.description: A Neolithic and Copper Age farming culture of Moldavia, Bessarabia and right-bank Ukraine, named after the village of Cucuteni near Iași, where it was first excavated in 1884. From about 5000 to 3500 BCE its people built villages of timber-and-clay houses — in Ukraine some of the largest settlements of their age in Europe — and made fine painted pottery in spirals and bands, figurines and copper tools. They often burned their houses on purpose before rebuilding. Further south, the Hamangia culture of Dobruja left the clay figure known as the “Thinker of Hamangia” (c. 5000 BCE) and the Gumelnița culture held the lower Danube. The culture is a timeline item and a pin, not a territorial outline.

items.name: Getae, Dacians and the Greek colonies
items.description: Greek settlers from Miletus founded Histria near the Danube mouths in the later 7th century BCE (traditionally 657 BCE), followed by Tomis (Constanța) and Callatis (Mangalia). Herodotus calls the Getae the bravest and most just of the Thracians; Darius I of Persia crossed their land in 514 BCE. In 292 BCE the Getic king Dromichaetes captured Lysimachus, one of Alexander’s successors, and let him go, and Celtic groups settled in Transylvania in the 4th–3rd centuries. Hill-fortresses and the cult of Zalmoxis mark the Dacian world inside the Carpathian arc; the Greek cities of the coast are pins, and the peoples’ layer shows the tribes.

periods.name: Getae and the Persian and Macedonian wars

items.name: Burebista’s Dacia
items.description: Burebista, a Getic–Dacian king with his centre in the Orăștie Mountains of Transylvania, united the tribes in the first half of the 1st century BCE. Strabo says that with the high priest Deceneus he reformed the people, cutting down the vines; he crushed the Boii and Taurisci on the middle Danube and, around 55–48 BCE, took the Greek cities from Olbia to Apollonia. Pompey sought his help against Caesar, and Caesar is said to have planned a war against him. Both men were murdered in 44 BCE, and Burebista’s realm broke into four or five parts. On the globe the Dacian kingdom starts with him (c. 82 BCE) and is at its peak around 60 BCE.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Dacian Fortresses of the Orastie Mountains

items.name: Decebalus and the Dacian Wars
items.description: Decebalus became king of the Dacians around 87 CE, after Dacian raids into Moesia killed its governor. He destroyed the army of Cornelius Fuscus at the first battle of Tapae (86/87); Domitian’s general Tettius Julianus won the second (88), but the peace of 89 left Decebalus a client paid by Rome. Trajan invaded in 101, won again at Tapae and forced terms in 102, keeping garrisons in the Banat and Oltenia; when Decebalus rebuilt his forces Trajan returned in 105 over Apollodorus’s bridge at Drobeta, took Sarmizegetusa Regia in 106, and Decebalus killed himself rather than be captured. Trajan’s Column in Rome tells the story in spiral reliefs.

items.name: Roman Dacia
items.description: Trajan made the conquered kingdom a province in 106, with its capital at Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa and the legion XIII Gemina at Apulum (Alba Iulia). Colonists came “from all the Roman world” (Eutropius) to work the gold mines of the Apuseni at Alburnus Maior and to farm; Napoca, Apulum, Porolissum, Drobeta and Romula grew into towns. Hadrian gave up the plain of Muntenia and southern Moldavia (117–118) and split Dacia; during the Marcomannic Wars (from 168) the three Daciae were put under one governor and V Macedonica moved to Potaissa. Under attack from the Goths and the Carpi, the province was abandoned by Aurelian (271–275), who gave the name Dacia to new provinces south of the Danube. Whether a Latin-speaking population stayed north of the river is the old continuity debate of Romanian history.

items.name: The migration age
items.description: After the Romans left, the lands north of the Danube were crossed and ruled in turn by Goths (the Sântana de Mureș–Chernyakhov culture, 4th century), Huns (from the 370s; the Pietroasele treasure was buried about then), Gepids in Transylvania, Avars (from 567) and Slavs, who settled widely from the 6th century. Byzantium held Dobruja again under Justinian; Constantine had briefly bridged the Danube at Sucidava in 328. The First Bulgarian Empire ruled the plain and Dobruja from the 8th–9th centuries, and Magyars, Pechenegs and later Cumans followed. Over these centuries the Romanian (Vlach) language formed from the Latin of the Balkan–Danube provinces. On the globe the peoples’ layer shows Goths, Slavs and steppe peoples; the Bulgarian shapes come from Day 88.

items.name: Medieval Transylvania
items.description: Transylvania was brought into the Kingdom of Hungary from around 1000 and ruled by a voivode. Hungarian kings settled German “Saxons” from the 1140s around Sibiu, Brașov and Bistrița, and the Székelys in the east; the Teutonic Knights held the Burzenland in 1211–1225. The Mongols burned the land in 1241. The Unio Trium Nationum (1438) shared power between the nobles, Saxons and Székelys and left the Romanian majority outside it after the Bobâlna revolt. John Hunyadi, voivode from 1441, led the crusades against the Ottomans and won at Belgrade in 1456; his son Matthias Corvinus, born at Cluj, became king of Hungary. After Mohács (1526) and the fall of Buda (1541) Transylvania went its own way. The kingdom of Hungary is not drawn on the globe in these centuries.

periods.name: Union of three nations and Hunyadi

items.name: Wallachia: Basarab I to Mircea the Elder
items.description: Small voivodeships between the southern Carpathians and the Danube, such as Litovoi’s in the 1270s, were united around 1310 by Basarab I, whose victory over Charles Robert of Hungary at Posada in 1330 made Wallachia independent. Its first courts were at Câmpulung and Curtea de Argeș, where the princely church still stands, and in 1359 Constantinople set up a metropolitan see for Ungro-Wallachia. Mircea the Elder (1386–1418) took Dobruja after the fall of its despots, fought Bayezid I at Rovine (1395) and joined the crusade of Nicopolis (1396); after Mehmed I took Dobruja (1417) Wallachia began to pay tribute to the Ottomans.

items.name: The founding of Moldavia
items.description: Moldavia began as a Hungarian march beyond the eastern Carpathians, set up after the campaigns against the Golden Horde around 1345–1347 and led by Dragoș from Maramureș. Bogdan I, another Maramureș voivode, crossed the mountains, threw out Dragoș’s heirs and made Moldavia independent by about 1359–1365. Its courts moved from Baia to Siret and Suceava; Roman I (c. 1392) styled himself ruler “from the mountains to the sea”, and Alexander the Good (1400–1432) gave it a long peace, a metropolis and trade on the road from Lviv to the Black Sea ports of Kilia and Cetatea Albă. Moldavia was claimed by both Hungary and Poland.

items.name: Despotate of Dobruja
items.description: On the Black Sea coast between the Danube and Varna, the boyar Balik and then his brother Dobrotitsa ruled from Karvuna and Kaliakra from the 1340s, with the Byzantine title of despot and under the nominal overlordship of Tarnovo. After Ivan Alexander’s realm split in 1356 they were on their own: Dobrotitsa took Varna, helped free Emperor John V in 1366–1367, fought the Genoese and tried to put his son-in-law on the throne of Trebizond. His son Ivanko made peace with Genoa in 1387 but lost Varna and Kaliakra to the Ottomans in 1388; Mircea of Wallachia held the north until Mehmed I took the land, about 1417. The despotate fills the gap left on the globe between the Second Bulgarian Empire (Day 88) and Mircea’s Dobruja.

items.name: Vlad III the Impaler
items.description: Vlad III, son of Vlad II Dracul and called Dracula after his father’s order of the Dragon, ruled Wallachia briefly in 1448, from 1456 to 1462 and again in 1476. He had grown up as an Ottoman hostage. In power he crushed rival boyars, raided the Saxon towns and, in 1461–1462, stopped paying tribute, burned the Ottoman Danube forts and, in the Night Attack of June 1462, tried to kill Mehmed II in his camp near Târgoviște. Mehmed installed Vlad’s brother Radu, and Matthias Corvinus held Vlad captive for years. His mass impalements, told in German pamphlets, made him notorious; he was killed fighting in late 1476 or early 1477. Bram Stoker borrowed his name in 1897.

periods.name: Second reign and the Night Attack

items.name: Stephen the Great
items.description: Stephen III of Moldavia ruled for 47 years (1457–1504). He beat Matthias Corvinus at Baia (1467) and an Ottoman army at Vaslui in January 1475 — called by Pope Sixtus IV a “champion of Christ” — but lost at Războieni (1476) and saw Kilia and Cetatea Albă fall to Bayezid II in 1484. He defeated the Poles in the Codrii Cosminului (1497). A chain of fortresses and dozens of churches and monasteries, from Putna, where he is buried, to Voroneț, were built in his reign; their painted walls followed under his son. Before he died he advised paying tribute to keep Moldavia’s autonomy, and in 1992 the Romanian Orthodox Church made him a saint.

items.name: Principality of Transylvania
items.description: After the fall of Buda (1541) the Ottomans let the eastern Hungarian kingdom of John Sigismund Zápolya survive as a tributary realm ruled from Alba Iulia; at the Treaty of Speyer (1570) he took the title of Prince of Transylvania. Its diets granted rare religious freedom: the Diet of Torda (1568) recognised the Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist and Unitarian churches. Stephen Báthory, prince from 1571, became king of Poland. Under Gabriel Bethlen (1613–1629) and George I Rákóczi it fought in the Thirty Years’ War, but George II Rákóczi’s invasion of Poland (1657) brought Ottoman and Tatar devastation. After the siege of Vienna the Habsburgs moved in: the Diploma Leopoldinum (1691) and the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) made it theirs, and the Peace of Szatmár (1711) ended Francis II Rákóczi’s war.

items.name: Michael the Brave’s union
items.description: Michael (Mihai Viteazul), prince of Wallachia from 1593, joined the Holy League against the Ottomans in 1594, killed his Ottoman creditors and beat Sinan Pasha at Călugăreni in 1595. In October 1599 he won Transylvania at Șelimbăr and entered Alba Iulia; in May 1600 he took Moldavia, and for a few months he called himself prince of Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia — the first time the three lands were ruled together. The Transylvanian nobles and the Habsburg general Giorgio Basta beat him at Mirăslău in September 1600, and the Poles drove him from Moldavia. Restored with Basta, he won at Guruslău in 1601 and was murdered on Basta’s orders at Câmpia Turzii in August 1601. In the 19th century his union became a symbol for the Romanian national movement.

items.name: The Phanariot century
items.description: After Dimitrie Cantemir of Moldavia sided with Peter the Great in 1711 and Constantin Brâncoveanu of Wallachia was executed in Constantinople in 1714, the Porte named Greek “Phanariot” princes from the Phanar district of the capital (Moldavia from 1711, Wallachia from 1716), often for a few years each. Some, like Constantine Mavrocordatos, abolished serfdom (1746, 1749). The Habsburgs held Oltenia in 1718–1739 and took Bukovina from Moldavia in 1775; Russia occupied the principalities in its Ottoman wars, won rights of protection at Küçük Kaynarca (1774) and annexed Bessarabia at the Treaty of Bucharest (1812). In Habsburg Transylvania, the uprising of Horea, Cloșca and Crișan (1784) and the Supplex Libellus Valachorum (1791) asked for Romanian rights.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Revolt of Horea, Cloșca and Crișan

items.name: Revolution, union and independence
items.description: Tudor Vladimirescu’s rising in Wallachia (1821), alongside the Greek Filiki Eteria, ended the Phanariot regime. After the Russo-Turkish war of 1828–1829 the Organic Statutes gave the principalities modern institutions under Russian protection, and the revolutions of 1848 failed. In 1859 both Moldavia and Wallachia elected Alexandru Ioan Cuza as prince, uniting them; the United Principalities took the name Romania, carried out land reform, and in 1866 brought in Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. Romania declared independence on 9 May 1877, fought beside Russia at Plevna, and was recognised at the Congress of Berlin (1878), gaining northern Dobruja; Carol I was crowned king in 1881. From 1815 the globe’s nations layer draws the Danubian Principalities and then Romania.

items.name: Kingdom of Romania
items.description: The kingdom crushed the great peasant revolt of 1907 and took southern Dobruja in the Second Balkan War (1913). It entered the First World War on the Allied side in 1916, lost Bucharest, and still emerged in 1918 with Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania (union proclaimed at Alba Iulia on 1 December 1918) — Greater Romania, confirmed at Trianon (1920). Land reform and the 1923 constitution followed, alongside the oil of Ploiești, King Carol II’s royal dictatorship (1938) and the fascist Iron Guard. In 1940 Romania lost Bessarabia and northern Bukovina to the USSR, northern Transylvania to Hungary and southern Dobruja to Bulgaria; under Ion Antonescu it fought beside Germany and killed or deported hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma, until King Michael’s coup of 23 August 1944 switched sides. Northern Transylvania returned in 1947, and the Communists forced Michael to abdicate on 30 December 1947.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Romania in World War II

items.name: Communist Romania
items.description: The Romanian People’s Republic, proclaimed on 30 December 1947, nationalised industry, collectivised farming and imprisoned hundreds of thousands in jails such as Sighet and Pitești and in labour on the Danube–Black Sea Canal; the Securitate watched everyone. Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej got Soviet troops out (1958) and began a line independent of Moscow. Nicolae Ceaușescu, leader from 1965, condemned the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia and was courted by the West, then built a personality cult, banned abortion (Decree 770, 1966), and paid off the foreign debt in the 1980s by rationing food, heat and light while building the vast House of the People in Bucharest. The revolution that began in Timișoara on 16 December 1989 overthrew him; he and his wife were executed on 25 December.

items.name: Modern Romania
items.description: After the December 1989 revolution the National Salvation Front of Ion Iliescu won the 1990 elections, and miners were brought into Bucharest against protesters (the mineriads). A new constitution came in 1991, and the 1996 election brought the first peaceful change of power. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union on 1 January 2007, with Bulgaria; millions of Romanians went to work abroad. Anti-corruption cases, the 2015 Colectiv club fire and the 2017 protests against easing corruption laws shaped politics. Romania joined the Schengen area by air and sea in March 2024 and fully on 1 January 2025; the presidential election of November 2024 was annulled, and Nicușor Dan won the rerun in May 2025.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Romania and the European Union
